entries.title: Stingray Sam
entries.what: Cory McAbee's black-and-white musical science-fiction serial, told in six ten-minute chapters: a lounge singer and his old partner the Quasar Kid cross several planets to rescue a kidnapped girl and earn a pardon
entries.why: McAbee writing, directing, scoring and starring again in the same deadpan space-western-musical idiom, with the same matte-painted cheapness and songs that stop the plot dead; the closest thing that exists to a sequel in register

entries.title: Crazy and Thief
entries.what: McAbee's 52-minute third feature, shot by himself: a seven-year-old girl leads her two-year-old brother on a navigational quest through New York using star graphics found on the pavement
entries.why: McAbee directing, writing, scoring and shooting, and songs again arrive without warning inside a non-musical world; grade and tone diverge because the film is in colour, tender, child-scaled and has no spacecraft, cowboys or professional actors, so a viewer chasing the monochrome grime will not find it here

entries.title: Deep Astronomy and the Romantic Sciences
entries.what: McAbee's 71-minute lecture-film: a man in a dive bar is tested by an android woman while a narrator delivers pseudo-scientific lectures, interrupted by songs, animations and fake commercials
entries.why: McAbee directing, narrating and singing, with the same flat-affect pseudo-expository voice that explains the wrong things at length and the right things not at all, and the same handmade graphic interludes

entries.title: The Phantom Empire
entries.what: Gene Autry's twelve-chapter Mascot serial, in which a singing cowboy running a radio dude ranch must get back to the microphone on schedule while fighting the underground radium kingdom of Murania
entries.why: The literal ancestor: the only earlier American film in which a cowboy sings on cue and then descends into a science-fiction world, and the one McAbee's interviewer reached for as 'Superman and the Mole Men meets Gene Autry'; the same tinny monochrome, the same ray-gun props visibly made of household objects, the same total refusal to acknowledge that the genres do not fit

entries.title: Space Is the Place
entries.what: Sun Ra lands a music-powered spacecraft, opens an employment agency in Oakland, plays the Overseer at cards for the fate of the Black race, and performs with the Arkestra throughout
entries.why: A blue-collar musician-hero moving between planets in a film that keeps stopping for full numbers played straight, built out of borrowed sets and costume-shop futurism, with a leading man whose deadpan cosmology is delivered as plain fact; the single closest match in American cinema for how the songs and the space travel coexist without either apologising, though it is in colour

entries.title: Forbidden Zone
entries.what: Richard Elfman's black-and-white musical, grown out of the Mystic Knights of the Oingo Boingo stage act: a girl falls through a door in a basement into the Sixth Dimension, ruled by a dwarf king and a frog butler, with thirteen numbers and Danny Elfman's first score
entries.why: The nearest thing to a sibling film: monochrome, made for about a hundred thousand dollars by a band, with painted flats standing in for a whole world and songs that arrive as if the film had forgotten it was not a musical; louder and ruder than McAbee, but the same conviction that cheapness is the style

entries.title: Dead Man
entries.what: Jim Jarmusch's black-and-white western: an accountant named William Blake travels west to a job that does not exist, is shot, and is escorted toward the water by an outcast Native man who believes he is the poet
entries.why: Black-and-white American western built out of long deadpan exchanges between men who talk past each other, with Neil Young's guitar arriving as an unexplained voice over the images the way McAbee's songs do; the same slow, episodic drift from one squalid outpost to the next

entries.title: Stranger Than Paradise
entries.what: Jarmusch's black-and-white debut in single-take scenes separated by blackouts: three characters drift from New York to Cleveland to Florida and nothing much happens anywhere
entries.why: The template for the American independent McAbee works inside: monochrome, made for almost nothing on short ends, structured as deadpan blocks with dead air left in, and funny precisely because it declines to explain itself or sell the joke

entries.title: Alphaville
entries.what: Godard's black-and-white science fiction: trench-coated agent Lemmy Caution drives into a distant city run by the computer Alpha 60 and shoots his way out, with no set or effect built for the film
entries.why: The proof that a science-fiction world can be made entirely out of tone, flat light and a gravelly narrating voice rather than money; the same noir-inflected monochrome, the same absurdist logic delivered in a bored monotone, the same hard-boiled hero misplaced in a genre he does not belong to

entries.title: Computer Chess
entries.what: Andrew Bujalski's film shot on 1969 analogue video tubes in black and white: programmers gather at a hotel for a man-versus-machine chess tournament while a couples-therapy retreat happens down the corridor
entries.why: The modern equivalent of McAbee's bet — a period science-fiction texture achieved by shooting on obsolete black-and-white equipment rather than dressing a set — with the same crowd of odd, flatly-performed men, the same jokes that land only if nobody signals them, and the same willingness to let a scene go strange without warning

entries.title: The Saddest Music in the World
entries.what: Guy Maddin's Depression-era fable, mostly in grainy black and white: a beer baroness with glass legs full of beer runs a contest to find the world's saddest music, and countries compete
entries.why: The other contemporary filmmaker critics reach for when describing McAbee, and rightly: an antique monochrome world assembled from backlot scraps, songs performed as contest turns inside a non-musical story, and absurd premises stated with complete sincerity and no wink

entries.title: Pennies from Heaven
entries.what: Herbert Ross's film of Dennis Potter's script, with Steve Martin as a Depression-era sheet-music salesman whose squalid life is punctuated by characters lip-syncing to period records in lavish studio fantasies
entries.why: McAbee names Potter as the reason he wanted to make musicals at all — 'I discovered Dennis Potter and his work, and I became really excited about the idea of making musicals' — and singles this one out: 'Pennies from Heaven with Steve Martin was amazing.' Grade and tone diverge sharply: it is glossy MGM-pastiche colour on a studio budget and ends in genuine cruelty, where McAbee is monochrome, cheap and kind

entries.title: Dark Star
entries.what: John Carpenter and Dan O'Bannon's student feature blown up to 35mm: four bored, filthy men on a twenty-year mission to blow up unstable planets, sharing the ship with a beachball alien and a bomb that argues phenomenology
entries.why: The founding blue-collar-labour-in-space comedy — men doing a tedious job in a grubby ship, bickering, with a country-western ballad ('Benson, Arizona') bookending the picture; McAbee's Samuel Curtis is the same kind of unglamorous interplanetary employee. Tone diverges: it is in colour and its humour is shaggier and more student-film than McAbee's flat, formal deadpan

entries.title: True Stories
entries.what: David Byrne narrates from a convertible as he tours the invented town of Virgil, Texas, during its sesquicentennial 'Celebration of Specialness', and the townspeople sing Talking Heads songs
entries.why: The American weird-regional film that most resembles McAbee's method: a deadpan host in western dress explaining an absurd world in a level, over-precise voice, with songs breaking out of the fabric of an ostensibly documentary-flat story. Tone is a 1 only because Byrne shoots in wide flat colour and the register is affectionate rather than grimy

entries.title: Superman and the Mole Men
entries.what: The 58-minute black-and-white B-feature that launched the Adventures of Superman series: George Reeves investigates the world's deepest oil well and finds small glowing subterranean men whom the townsfolk form a mob to hunt
entries.why: The exact texture McAbee's film pastiches — cheap monochrome fifties science fiction, a short feature shot flat and fast, with matte work and props obviously improvised. Named in the RogerEbert.com interview as part of the 'Superman and the Mole Men meets Gene Autry' description put to McAbee, which he took up rather than corrected (note: the phrasing is the interviewer Simon Abrams', not McAbee's own)

entries.title: It's Always Fair Weather
entries.what: Gene Kelly and Stanley Donen's CinemaScope musical: three war buddies reunite ten years later, find they cannot stand each other, and dance on roller skates through Manhattan
entries.why: Named in the RogerEbert.com interview's 'Aelita Queen of Mars meets It's Always Fair Weather' formulation, and structurally apt — a musical about disappointed men whose old bond has curdled, which is what McAbee's Curtis and Professor Hess are. Grade and tone diverge completely: this is wide-screen Technicolor MGM at full expense, brassy and polished, the opposite of the thing McAbee's film feels like (and the phrasing is the interviewer's, not McAbee's)

entries.title: Aelita
entries.what: Yakov Protazanov's Soviet silent: a Moscow engineer dreams his way to Mars, where the queen Aelita watches him through a telescope and a workers' revolt breaks out among the Martian labouring class
entries.why: The first film to put class and manual labour in space, with Constructivist Mars built out of angular flats that read as drawings rather than places — the same declared artifice as McAbee's painted spaceflight mattes. Cited in the RogerEbert.com interview's shorthand for McAbee's work. Tone is a 1: silent, grand and earnest, without the deadpan joke-timing

entries.title: Brimstone and Treacle
entries.what: Richard Loncraine's film of Dennis Potter's play: Sting plays a charming young drifter who insinuates himself into a suburban household caring for their brain-damaged daughter
entries.why: McAbee discusses this Potter adaptation directly in the RogerEbert.com interview — 'It's very dated, but there are parts of it that are pretty great' — confirming how far into Potter's filmography he had gone. Grade and tone diverge hard: it is colour, claustrophobic domestic English nastiness with almost no songs, and shares nothing of McAbee's texture except the author it descends from

entries.title: Eraserhead
entries.what: David Lynch's black-and-white debut, made over five years: Henry Spencer lives in an industrial wasteland, is handed a wailing deformed infant, and watches a woman sing in his radiator
entries.why: Included on formal grounds only — the deep-black monochrome, the industrial drone, the long silences and the woman who simply begins singing in the radiator are the texture McAbee shares. McAbee explicitly rejects it as an influence: 'because it's in black and white people sometimes say Eraserhead, but other than the fact that it's in black and white I don't really see much.' Never present this as a stated influence

entries.title: Plan 9 from Outer Space
entries.what: Ed Wood's black-and-white science fiction: aliens resurrect the dead in a Californian cemetery to stop humanity building the doomsday weapon Solaranite, with hubcap flying saucers and cardboard headstones
entries.why: Ed Wood is on McAbee's own list of influences for the film. This is the monochrome cheap-effects grammar McAbee quotes deliberately rather than falls into — flat lighting, visible strings, cosmic exposition delivered by a man standing still on an empty set — and the earnestness under it is exactly what makes McAbee's version affectionate rather than mocking

entries.title: Down by Law
entries.what: Jarmusch's black-and-white picaresque shot by Robby Müller: a DJ, a pimp and an Italian tourist share a New Orleans cell, escape, and wander the swamp bickering
entries.why: Three mismatched men stuck together in gorgeous high-contrast monochrome, with Tom Waits songs opening and closing as a voice from outside the story; the comedy comes from flat delivery and long waits, and the world is built from what was already there — all of it McAbee's register

entries.title: Way Out West
entries.what: Laurel and Hardy in black and white, delivering a gold-mine deed to the wrong woman in the town of Brushwood Gulch, stopping twice to sing and soft-shoe
entries.why: Entertainment Weekly's line on McAbee's film was 'imagine a Laurel and Hardy skit directed by Salvador Dali', and this is the Laurel and Hardy in question: a monochrome western where two incompetent men in the wrong clothes break into 'Trail of the Lonesome Pine' as if it were the natural next thing, which is precisely how McAbee stages a number

entries.title: Putney Swope
entries.what: Robert Downey Sr.'s mostly black-and-white satire: the token Black executive is accidentally elected chairman of a Madison Avenue agency, renames it Truth and Soul, and the commercials he makes are shot in colour
entries.why: American underground absurdism at its driest — scenes built as sketches, dialogue dubbed flat and wrong on purpose, monochrome punctured by inserted colour set-pieces the way McAbee punctures his film with numbers and montage; the cheapness is worn as attitude, not hidden

entries.title: Greaser's Palace
entries.what: Robert Downey Sr.'s acid western: a zoot-suited drifter called Jessy parachutes into the New Mexico desert, heals the sick, tap-dances on water and auditions for a saloon owner, en route to his own crucifixion
entries.why: A western in which the messiah is a song-and-dance man and everyone treats the mixture as unremarkable; the deadpan cruelty, the episodic outpost-to-outpost structure and the stage-act numbers dropped into a frontier landscape are directly McAbee's shape. Tone is a 1: it is in colour and considerably more scatological and hostile

entries.title: Hundreds of Beavers
entries.what: Mike Cheslik's near-silent black-and-white slapstick made in Wisconsin for about $150,000: a ruined applejack salesman becomes a fur trapper and wages escalating war on beavers played by people in mascot costumes
entries.why: The clearest current proof of McAbee's thesis that visible cheapness plus total commitment reads as style: monochrome, regional American, effects that announce themselves as hand-made, and a world whose rules are absurd and never once explained to the audience

entries.title: Clerks
entries.what: Kevin Smith's black-and-white debut, shot for around $27,000 in the convenience store where he worked: a day of customers, arguments and a hockey game on the roof
entries.why: The Sundance black-and-white American independent as a category — made on credit cards in one location, structured as titled chapters of digression, with the monochrome a budget necessity turned into the film's identity, exactly as McAbee's was

entries.title: In the Soup
entries.what: Alexandre Rockwell's black-and-white comedy, Sundance Grand Jury Prize winner: a broke would-be filmmaker advertises his 500-page script and is adopted by a charming gangster who promises to produce it
entries.why: The black-and-white Sundance independent McAbee's film descends from institutionally — a film about scraping a film together, shot in the cheapest available register with a flat, funny, unsentimental affect. Tone is a 1: its world is naturalistic New York rather than an invented one

entries.title: The Notorious Bettie Page
entries.what: Mary Harron's biography of the fifties pin-up, shot largely in period black and white with bursts of Miami colour, premiered at Sundance
entries.why: Shot by W. Mott Hupfel III, the cinematographer of The American Astronaut, and the closest his other work comes to it: the same conscious fifties monochrome pastiche and the same interest in cheap studio artifice as a look. Tone is a 1 — Harron's film is calm and biographical, with none of the deadpan absurdity

entries.title: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
entries.what: The Python troupe's Arthurian comedy, made for almost nothing in Scotland: knights mime horses with coconuts, and Terry Gilliam's cut-out animations carry the transitions
entries.why: Monty Python is on McAbee's stated list of influences, and the film's cut-out montage sequences were repeatedly compared to Gilliam's animation; the shared method is an epic world declared rather than afforded, with the audience expected to accept the substitution and laugh at nothing being underlined. Tone is a 1: colour, verbally frantic where McAbee is quiet

entries.title: Six-String Samurai
entries.what: Lance Mungia's post-apocalyptic road picture: a Buddy Holly lookalike with a guitar and a sword walks across the Nevada desert toward Lost Vegas to claim the throne of the dead King
entries.why: Reached for directly in critical writing on McAbee ('somewhere between Six-String Samurai and Dead Man, but science fiction musical'): a musician-gunfighter crossing a wasteland in a genre mash nobody asked for, made cheap and played straight. Tone is a 1 — saturated colour, faster cutting, a rock-video energy McAbee never uses

entries.title: Repo Man
entries.what: Alex Cox's Los Angeles science fiction: a punk drifts into car repossession and onto the trail of a Chevy Malibu with something lethal glowing in the boot
entries.why: Deadpan American absurdism where working-class labour, punk songs and an unexplained science-fiction object share one frame without the film ever reconciling them; the flat, mock-philosophical monologues from minor characters are McAbee's exact comic instrument. Tone is a 1: colour, and louder

entries.title: Outland
entries.what: Peter Hyams's science fiction on Io: a federal marshal uncovers an amphetamine racket keeping the titanium miners productive, and waits alone for killers to arrive on the shuttle
entries.why: The canonical blue-collar-labour-in-space picture and a direct High Noon transposition, which is the exact double genre-graft McAbee performs; its mining company town is the industrial-solar-system economy his film assumes. Tone is a 0: expensive, dim colour, humourless, and everything is explained

entries.title: Moon
entries.what: Duncan Jones's debut: a single contract worker finishing a three-year helium-3 mining stint on the far side of the Moon discovers what the company has actually been doing
entries.why: The modern anchor of the lonely-worker-in-space line McAbee sits in — one man, a long contract, a corporate errand, no glamour. Tone is a 0: it is in clean colour, melancholy and sincere throughout, with no songs, no jokes and a plot that resolves itself carefully

entries.title: Silent Running
entries.what: Douglas Trumbull's film: a botanist on a freighter carrying Earth's last forests refuses the order to destroy them, kills his crewmates and tends the dome with three repurposed maintenance drones
entries.why: A working freighter crewed by bored men playing cards, a hippie protagonist who does not belong in his job, and Joan Baez songs dropped whole over the images as an outside voice — the same trick McAbee's numbers play. Tone is a 0: colour, slow and openly sentimental where McAbee is dry

entries.title: Dancer in the Dark
entries.what: Lars von Trier's musical: a going-blind Czech factory worker in Washington State escapes into song sequences built from the rhythm of machinery, on her way to the gallows
entries.why: The other major contemporary film where songs erupt inside a world that is emphatically not a musical, and where the numbers are the character's private property rather than the film's — McAbee's stated distinction about his own songs. Tone is a 0: handheld digital colour, deafening and emotionally brutal, the opposite of McAbee's cool flatness

entries.title: The Brother from Another Planet
entries.what: John Sayles's cheap science fiction: a mute Black alien escapee with three toes crashes on Ellis Island, settles in Harlem, and is pursued by two absurd white bounty hunters in black
entries.why: American independent science fiction made for nothing, with the effects limited to what a prop and a cut can do, comedy built from long deadpan exchanges, and an outsider carrying an errand through a series of small rooms; the two pursuers are Professor Hess's comic register almost exactly. Tone is a 1 for colour and its warmer, more naturalistic street texture

entries.title: Gummo
entries.what: Harmony Korine's portrait of tornado-flattened Xenia, Ohio, assembled from vignettes: boys hunting cats to sell, a boy in pink bunny ears, a kitchen-sink bath, mixed film stocks and found footage
entries.why: The American weird-regional film at its most uncompromising — a place presented as an alien planet without explanation, built from non-actors and scavenged formats, with scenes that simply stop. McAbee's Ceres dance hall and the boy who saw a woman's breast belong to the same Americana. Tone is a 1: colour, formally scrappier and genuinely ugly where McAbee is composed

entries.title: Cry-Baby
entries.what: John Waters's fifties Baltimore musical: the delinquent Drapes and the square Squares sing at each other, with Johnny Depp as a rockabilly hero who sheds a single perfect tear
entries.why: A musical built entirely on the pleasure of period pastiche delivered in a flat, knowing, non-sung-through register, where the numbers punctuate rather than carry the story and every cheap effect is left visible; the rockabilly-cowboy hero and the deadpan Americana are McAbee's furniture. Tone is a 1: colour, broad and camp rather than dry

entries.title: Metropolis
entries.what: Fritz Lang's silent epic: the sons of the elite play above ground while workers operate the machines below, and a false Maria is built to incite them
entries.why: German Expressionism is on McAbee's stated list of influences, and this is its science-fiction monument — the vertical class geography of a machine society and the graphic, near-abstract black-and-white compositions his spaceflight mattes echo. Tone is a 1: monochrome and stylised, but enormous, silent and solemn

entries.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
entries.what: Robert Wiene's silent film with sets, shadows and even light painted directly onto flats: a showman exhibits a somnambulist at a fair, and murders follow
entries.why: The origin of the technique McAbee reaches for when he paints his outer space rather than building it — the acknowledgement that a backdrop is a drawing, and the refusal to pretend otherwise. German Expressionism is among his stated influences. Tone is a 1: the artifice matches, but there is no comedy and no music in McAbee's sense

entries.title: Gold Diggers of 1933
entries.what: Mervyn LeRoy's Warner Bros. backstage musical with Busby Berkeley numbers, ending with 'Remember My Forgotten Man' and its ranks of Depression veterans
entries.why: Busby Berkeley is named among McAbee's influences, and the Ceres dance-hall sequence takes its geometry from Berkeley's overhead patterning of identical bodies. Grade and tone diverge: this is a studio musical with a full orchestra and a plot that stops for spectacle, nothing like the dry chamber scale of McAbee's film

entries.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show
entries.what: Jim Sharman's film of the stage show: a straight couple break down outside a castle where an alien transvestite scientist from Transsexual, Transylvania is building a man
entries.why: Used in contemporary shorthand for McAbee's film ('a cross between The Rocky Horror Picture Show and The Grapes of Wrath'), and a real cousin — a band's stage act turned into a science-fiction musical made from thrift-store props and old B-movie iconography. Tone is a 1: colour, camp, loud, and it flatters the audience in a way McAbee never does

entries.title: One from the Heart
entries.what: Francis Ford Coppola's Las Vegas romance, built entirely on Zoetrope soundstages, in which a couple separate over a Fourth of July weekend while Tom Waits and Crystal Gayle sing commentary from outside the story
entries.why: The purest example of the trick McAbee uses — songs that belong to the film rather than the characters, sung by voices nobody in the story can hear, over a world openly declared as a built set. Tone is a 0: hot neon colour and a ruinously expensive studio gloss, where McAbee's artifice is poor and grey

entries.title: Popeye
entries.what: Robert Altman's musical with Harry Nilsson songs, shot in a full-scale Sweethaven built on Malta: Popeye arrives looking for his father and everyone mutters over each other
entries.why: A musical whose songs are half-swallowed, unresolved and sung by people who cannot really sing, set in a world built plank by plank and photographed as obviously constructed; the mumbling, overlapping deadpan is close to McAbee's refusal to sell a line. Tone is a 1: colour and busy, but it shares the handmade-world commitment

entries.title: Harry and Tonto
entries.what: Paul Mazursky's road picture: an elderly New Yorker evicted from his apartment crosses America with his cat, meeting people episodically as he goes
entries.why: McAbee names it unprompted as the kind of film he wants to make: 'Harry and Tonto — I love that film. It's actually a really strong, smart, gutsy film, but it's very kind. And that's what I look for in films.' The episodic string of encounters and the refusal to punish anyone is McAbee's structure. Grade and tone diverge completely: warm seventies colour naturalism, no genre, no songs

entries.title: Ed Wood
entries.what: Tim Burton's black-and-white biography of the director of Plan 9, shot in glossy fifties monochrome, with Martin Landau as Bela Lugosi
entries.why: About the sensibility McAbee names as an influence, and about the exact proposition his film embodies: that conviction and a cardboard tombstone can stand in for money. Tone is a 1 — it is monochrome and affectionate, but it is a polished studio picture that explains its subject carefully

entries.title: Alien
entries.what: Ridley Scott's film: the crew of the commercial towing vehicle Nostromo, arguing about bonuses and shares, are diverted to answer a signal
entries.why: The film that established the space freighter as a workplace and its crew as unionised labour rather than explorers — the economic universe McAbee's interplanetary trader operates in, and the reason his hero has cargo and a route rather than a mission. Tone is a 0: dark colour, meticulous, terrifying, with no comedy and no songs

entries.title: Slacker
entries.what: Richard Linklater's Austin film, which hands the camera from one talker to the next across a single day and never returns to anyone
entries.why: The American regional independent as method — a city rendered as a cast of monologuing eccentrics, made for nothing with friends, its structure a chain of handoffs rather than a plot; McAbee's film is likewise a chain of transactions. Tone is a 1: colour, conversational and unstylised

entries.title: Schizopolis
entries.what: Steven Soderbergh's self-financed comedy in which he plays two identical men, dialogue is replaced by functional descriptions of speech, and the film introduces itself to the audience from a stage
entries.why: A studio director spending his own money on formal jokes nobody asked for, with flat affect, non-sequitur structure and an announcer's voice addressing the viewer directly — McAbee's presentational deadpan in a different key. Tone is a 1: colour, more frantic, and more interested in language than in songs

entries.title: Pi
entries.what: Darren Aronofsky's high-contrast black-and-white debut, made for about $60,000 on reversal stock: a paranoid number theorist hunting a pattern in the stock market is pursued by Wall Street and by Kabbalists
entries.why: The other landmark grainy black-and-white Sundance science fiction of the period, shot on almost nothing with the harshness of the stock made into the film's whole look. Tone is a 1: the monochrome and the poverty match, but it is relentless, migraine-paced and utterly humourless

entries.title: Even Dwarfs Started Small
entries.what: Werner Herzog's black-and-white film with an all-dwarf cast: the inmates of a remote island institution revolt, and spend the film laughing at a driverless car going in circles
entries.why: Grade is only a 1 — no documented connection, and its cruelty is far from McAbee's kindness — but tone is a 2: stark high-contrast monochrome, an enclosed absurd world whose rules are never explained, and long deadpan sequences held past the point of comfort. Exactly the texture, almost none of the lineage

entries.title: The Ballad of Buster Scruggs
entries.what: The Coens' six-part western anthology, opening with a white-suited singing cowboy who shoots men dead between verses and ends the segment ascending with a harp
entries.why: The first chapter is the singing-cowboy-as-killer premise McAbee's Samuel Curtis inhabits, played with the same straight face, and the episodic structure of separate deaths matches his outpost-to-outpost chain. Tone is a 1: lush digital colour and a polished, expensive finish

entries.title: High Noon
entries.what: Fred Zinnemann's black-and-white western in near-real time: a marshal on his wedding day cannot find a single townsman to stand with him against the killers arriving on the noon train
entries.why: The western template the space-western line runs on — Outland is its direct transposition — and the source of the structure McAbee inverts, where a pursued man moves and a pursuer arrives on schedule. Listed on lineage only: I found no statement in which McAbee names it, contrary to the brief. Tone is a 0: austere, tense and entirely sincere, with its one Tex Ritter ballad used as conventional scoring

entries.title: Brand Upon the Brain!
entries.what: Guy Maddin's black-and-white silent-style autobiography, shot on Super 8 in nine days and originally toured with live narration, orchestra and Foley artists: a man returns to the island orphanage his parents ran
entries.why: Grade 1 because the connection is formal kinship rather than any documented link, but tone 2: grainy monochrome, frantic hand-made effects, a world of invented rules delivered flat, and a film conceived as a live band-and-performance event — which is how The Billy Nayer Show grew this material

entries.title: Space Truckers
entries.what: Stuart Gordon's film: one of the last independent haulage operators takes an unexamined load to Earth and finds he is carrying a shipment of killer robots
entries.why: The most literal statement of the premise McAbee builds on — an independent interplanetary trader moving cargo he should not have accepted, in a solar system that is entirely a freight economy. Tone is a 1: colour, broad and effects-driven, though the deliberately rubbery hardware has a kindred cheapness

entries.title: Head
entries.what: Bob Rafelson and Jack Nicholson's anti-film for the Monkees: the band dismantle their own image across disconnected sketches, war footage, a Western, a desert and a black box
entries.why: McAbee talks at length in the RogerEbert.com interview about the Monkees and about Micky Dolenz as 'such an amazing character', and this is what a band made when handed a film: numbers dropped into unrelated genre pastiches with no connective tissue, cheapness and self-awareness in the same gesture. Tone is a 1 — colour, psychedelic and busier than McAbee's flat frames

entries.title: The Savages
entries.what: Tamara Jenkins's drama with Laura Linney and Philip Seymour Hoffman: two estranged siblings move their dementia-stricken father into a Buffalo nursing home
entries.why: Shot by W. Mott Hupfel III, and the film for which he received his second Independent Spirit cinematography nomination after The American Astronaut, so it shows what the same eye does with naturalism. Grade and tone diverge as far as they can: a muted-colour domestic drama with nothing of McAbee's register in it at all

entries.title: La Jetée
entries.what: Chris Marker's 28-minute black-and-white science fiction told almost entirely in still photographs, with a narrator: a prisoner in post-war Paris is sent through time toward a memory from the jetty at Orly
entries.why: The proof that science fiction can be made from stills, a voice and no sets at all — the same economy that lets McAbee paint his spaceflight. Tone is a 1: the austere monochrome matches, but the film is elegiac and entirely without jokes or songs

entries.title: Stalker
entries.what: Tarkovsky's three-hander: a guide leads a writer and a scientist on foot through a forbidden Zone toward a room said to grant wishes
entries.why: The defensible link is structural, not tonal: a journey across a forbidden geography carried by walking and talk rather than by effects, in a science fiction that has no spectacle in it and never wanted one. Everything else pulls apart. The grounds offered here, meditative and slow-burn, describe the opposite of a ninety-one-minute deadpan musical that stops for a barn dance and a song about the boy who actually saw a woman's breast. Stalker is also the reflex answer to any question about art-house science fiction, which is part of why it turned up.

entries.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
entries.what: Tsukamoto's 16mm black-and-white body horror, in which a Tokyo salaryman's flesh erupts into scrap metal, shot in pixilated bursts over an industrial score
entries.why: Shares the two things most visible about The American Astronaut from the outside: no budget, and no colour. There is also a real kinship in both directors being their own band. But McAbee's monochrome is stage-lit and still, cut for comic timing, while Tsukamoto's is a shrieking assault with no jokes, no songs and no pauses. The key already holds Eraserhead at this junction, which is the same industrial texture with the deadpan attached.

entries.title: Santa Sangre
entries.what: Jodorowsky's Mexican-Italian melodrama about a circus boy who becomes the arms of his armless mother and kills at her direction
entries.why: Sits in the midnight-movie lineage The American Astronaut plays to, and shares a taste for troupe performers and sacred nonsense delivered straight, which is the same ground the key's Rocky Horror entry occupies at this grade. But Jodorowsky is operatic, bloody and saturated where McAbee is dry, chaste and flat, and of the Jodorowsky films this is the furthest from him: El Topo, with its deadpan Western grammar, would have been the pick.

entries.title: The City of Lost Children
entries.what: Jeunet and Caro's designed dystopia, in which a fairground strongman searches for his stolen brother in a port city where a scientist harvests children's dreams
entries.why: Both build an entire retro-future out of handmade parts and populate it with a gallery of grotesque turns rather than characters, and both expect an audience to accept an invented world without a word of explanation. The difference is money and density: Jeunet and Caro stuff the frame to its corners and light it like a fairground, where McAbee gives you a bare stage, two people and a song. Worth recommending for the shared appetite for invented worlds and little else.

entries.title: Hardware
entries.what: Richard Stanley's debut: a scavenged war-droid head reassembles itself inside a Brutalist apartment and kills its way out, scored by Simon Boswell with Iggy Pop and Ministry on the soundtrack
entries.why: One specific thing carries. Both futures are welded together out of junk because junk was what the budget allowed, and both directors came out of music rather than film school. Past that the recommendation misfires: Hardware is a slasher confined to one flat, all red filters and grinding noise, and The American Astronaut is a picaresque comedy shot wide and dry. The oppressive visual style offered as the reason describes a film McAbee did not make.

entries.title: Phase IV
entries.what: Saul Bass's only feature: two scientists sealed in an Arizona research dome are studied and outmanoeuvred by an ant colony that has begun acting as a single mind
entries.why: No connection beyond both being cult science fiction made outside the studio system. Phase IV is humourless and macro-photographic, built on a scientific premise pursued to an abstract ending; The American Astronaut is vaudeville in space with musical numbers and a running joke about a cat. Isolation and strange evolution, the grounds given, are not subjects this target has. It is a fine film and it earns its place in the Call of Cthulhu list, where the same model also suggested it.

entries.title: A Field in England
entries.what: Wheatley's black-and-white Civil War picture: deserters press-ganged into digging for treasure in a single field eat mushrooms and come apart
entries.why: The nearest thing in recent cinema to McAbee's method: a monochrome genre film made for nothing out of a handful of actors, one location and a premise stated flatly, with period-flavoured comic dialogue that turns without warning into a formal set piece. Both trust the audience to accept an invented rulebook on sight. Tone parts in the last third, where Wheatley goes into real horror and McAbee never stops being funny.

entries.title: Songs from the Second Floor
entries.what: Roy Andersson's first feature in twenty-five years: fixed-camera tableaux of a European city in gridlock, including a man who has burned down his own furniture business
entries.why: Both films are built the same way, out of composed static frames in which drab people perform absurd business with total commitment and no wink, and both hold the deadpan long enough that the laugh and the dread arrive together. Andersson's greenish-grey palette does in colour what McAbee's stage-lit monochrome does in black-and-white. A genuinely good pick the key had missed: Andersson is absent from this list entirely, and he is the closest living relative to the film's comic register.

entries.title: The Happiness of the Katakuris
entries.what: Miike's musical: a family running a mountain guest house sings and dances its way through the disposal of guests who keep dying, with claymation interludes
entries.why: The other 2001 cult film that answers a genre problem by breaking into song, and it works the same trick, staging musical numbers dead straight inside a grim situation and folding the cheapness of the effects into the joke. Both refuse to settle their register, moving between sincerity and absurdity inside a single scene. Miike is broader and louder, in colour and pitched at family comedy, where McAbee stays dry throughout.

entries.title: Delicatessen
entries.what: Jeunet and Caro's debut: the tenants of a post-apocalyptic apartment block are butchered and sold by the landlord downstairs, in sepia and slapstick
entries.why: A comic post-apocalypse assembled out of junk and carried by rhythm rather than plot. Its best-known sequence times an entire building's noises to a squeaking bed, which is the kind of number McAbee builds whole scenes around, and both films take a bleak premise and play it as physical comedy rather than horror. Its density and its colour keep it a step away from The American Astronaut's bare stage.

entries.title: Hard to Be a God
entries.what: Aleksei German's last film, from the Strugatsky brothers' novel: an observer from Earth lives among the filth of a planet stalled in its own Middle Ages, in 177 black-and-white minutes
entries.why: Shares nothing with the target but the absence of colour. German's film is an immersion designed to exhaust, a camera shoved through mud, spit and offal for three hours with no distance and no relief; The American Astronaut is flat, brisk and stage-bound, and keeps the viewer at arm's length on purpose. Pairing two films because both are monochrome is matching on a lab result, not a connection.

entries.title: Rubber
entries.what: Dupieux's desert comedy: a discarded tyre comes to life, discovers it can make heads explode, and is watched throughout by an on-screen audience with binoculars
entries.why: The same comic engine. An absurd premise is announced without apology and then obeyed to the letter by actors who never concede that anything is odd, in flat desert light and on almost no money. Dupieux's 'no reason' monologue is the manifesto for the kind of worldbuilding McAbee does when he lays out the interplanetary economy around the boy who saw a woman's breast. Rubber is knowing in a way McAbee is not: its subject is the audience, where his sincerity inside the nonsense is total.

entries.title: The Falls
entries.what: Greenaway's 185-minute mock-directory: ninety-two biographies of people affected by the Violent Unknown Event, recited in flat documentary style
entries.why: Defensible for one specific pleasure both films offer, an invented cosmology delivered deadpan as settled fact, with taxonomies, statistics and names presented as though the audience already agreed to them. That is exactly how The American Astronaut hands over its solar system. Against it: The Falls is a three-hour structuralist list with no characters and no story, and pointing someone who enjoyed a ninety-minute musical at it is a very large ask.

entries.title: Dark City
entries.what: Proyas's noir science fiction: a man wakes beside a corpse in a city where aliens rebuild the streets and the inhabitants' memories every night
entries.why: Pulled in by the words 'artificial world' and by its own standing as a 1990s cult object. Dark City is a studio picture with expensive expressionist sets, a paranoid mystery and constant menace; The American Astronaut has bare stages, no mystery and no menace at all. The key does already list Dark City where it belongs, under Avalon, which is a film actually about a constructed reality.

entries.title: Coherence
entries.what: James Ward Byrkit's single-location improvised film: eight friends at a dinner party during a comet pass discover the houses on their street are branching copies of each other, and begin swapping between them
entries.why: Joined to the target by budget and genre shelf and by nothing else. Coherence is a naturalistic present-day puzzle film whose whole pleasure is working out a rule system the characters are working out alongside you; The American Astronaut states its rules flatly in the first ten minutes — the interplanetary trade in a corpse, the cat, the boy who actually saw a woman's breast — and never once treats them as a mystery. The key already covers micro-budget American science fiction properly with Computer Chess and Crazy and Thief, both of which share McAbee's formal peculiarity and not merely his shooting schedule. 'Low-budget, cerebral, dialogue-driven' describes a production, not a film.

entries.title: Sunshine
entries.what: Danny Boyle's mission film: a crew carrying a stellar bomb to reignite a dying sun loses its discipline, and then a passenger, on the approach
entries.why: A studio picture with a forty-million-dollar effects budget, an orchestral-electronic score deployed for awe, and a third act that turns into a slasher. Nothing in it is deadpan, nothing is handmade, nothing is sung. The ground offered — existential science fiction with deep themes — would attach Sunshine to several hundred films, and The American Astronaut is not in fact interested in existential themes; it is interested in a man delivering a body across the solar system and singing a song about it on the way.

entries.title: Arrival
entries.what: Denis Villeneuve's first-contact drama: a linguist is brought to a Montana landing site to translate the written language of heptapods, whose grammar has no tense
entries.why: The reflex prestige answer to any question containing the words 'intelligent science fiction'. It is a grave, beautifully graded, emotionally engineered studio film about grief and determinism. The American Astronaut is a black-and-white vaudeville in which a man wins a viewing of a woman's breast in a space bar and pays for his passage in dance. There is no axis on which the two meet, and 'atmospheric, dialogue-heavy' is not an axis.

entries.title: Annihilation
entries.what: Alex Garland's adaptation of the VanderMeer novel: a biologist enters a coastal zone where the rules governing living forms refract and recombine
entries.why: Suggested on 'grounded sci-fi realism', which is not a quality this target has or wants — its ships are stage sets and its planets are backdrops, on purpose. Garland's film is a solemn, effects-led study of self-destruction that ends in ten minutes of wordless spectacle; McAbee's is flat, cheap, funny and sung. Annihilation is a perfectly good recommendation and already sits in the Call of Cthulhu key, on the cosmic-indifference ground it genuinely serves. Here it is only a well-regarded recent science fiction title.

entries.title: The Thing
entries.what: John Carpenter's Antarctic siege film: an organism thawed out of the ice imitates the men of an American research station one at a time
entries.why: Isolation and paranoia are the grounds offered and neither belongs to this target. Samuel Curtis's difficulty is not that he cannot trust the people he meets, it is that every one of them is delighted to see him and immediately starts singing. Carpenter's film is a tightly wound horror picture carrying the most expensive practical creature work of its decade; the target's effects budget went on a plywood rocket and a barn. The Thing is a strong recommendation for The Call of Cthulhu and is rated there on a documented link; against this film it is a genre label with a famous title attached.

entries.title: Ad Astra
entries.what: James Gray's space film: an astronaut travels out to Neptune to find the father whose antimatter experiment is destabilising the solar system
entries.why: A hundred-million-dollar film built on whispered voice-over about a son's feelings, which is the one register The American Astronaut refuses absolutely — its emotional scenes are songs, and its songs are straight lines. The shared noun is 'space'. That a solitary man travels between planets is true and worthless: Silent Running does that too, and the key holds it because it also shares the junk-built ships, the working-stiff hero and the melancholy comedy.

entries.title: The Fountain
entries.what: Darren Aronofsky's three-strand film: a conquistador, a research oncologist and a bald man in a floating bubble tree all play out the same refusal of death
entries.why: Chosen for the words 'philosophical' and 'visually poetic'. Aronofsky's film is rapturous, golden, scored for swelling strings and entirely sincere about transcendence; the target is monochrome, flat, and treats every sincerity it produces as the setup for a joke it never bothers to land. Note that the key does hold Aronofsky — through Pi, which earns its place on grain, poverty and monomania, the three qualities The Fountain spent thirty-five million dollars not having.

entries.title: Gravity
entries.what: Alfonso Cuarón's survival film: an astronaut cut loose from a destroyed shuttle works her way down through two stations to re-entry
entries.why: An immersive technical spectacle whose entire value is photographic realism and sustained physical tension, offered to a film whose ship interiors are lit like a small theatre and whose most elaborate sequence is a barn dance. This is the clearest case in the batch of a famous title arriving because the target was filed under 'space'.

entries.title: Contact
entries.what: Robert Zemeckis's adaptation of Carl Sagan: a radio astronomer receives a signal from Vega carrying the plans for a machine, and has to argue it through committees
entries.why: Offered as 'intellectual, slow-burn, existential sci-fi with dialogue'. Every one of those words is doing work the target never asked for. Contact is an earnest mainstream picture about faith and evidence with a large cast of senators and a news-footage montage; The American Astronaut has four locations, a band, and no argument to make about anything at all. Genre shelf only.

entries.title: The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension
entries.what: W.D. Richter's cult film: a neurosurgeon, particle physicist and rock musician and his Hong Kong Cavaliers repel an invasion of Red Lectroids from Planet 10, with John Lithgow as Lord John Whorfin
entries.why: A real match on the thing that matters most here. An entire cosmology — Yoyodyne, the Oscillation Overthruster, the Black Lectroid ultimatum, the rule that all the invaders are called John — is handed over as settled fact by people who never pause to explain any of it, and the hero's band performs in the film as itself. That is exactly how McAbee delivers his solar system, the corpse-and-cat economy, and the Billy Nayer Show as both cast and score. It belongs beside the key's Repo Man and Forbidden Zone. Richter's film is a colour studio picture that mugs and shouts, where McAbee's comedy is dry and almost motionless, which is where the tone parts.

entries.title: The Lost Skeleton of Cadavra
entries.what: Larry Blamire's pastiche of 1950s poverty-row science fiction: a scientist, his wife, two aliens and a woman assembled out of forest animals converge on a meteorite of atmospherium. Shot on video and converted to black-and-white; indexed at 2001, its festival year, with US theatrical release only in March 2004
entries.why: The other 2001 monochrome cult film, and it runs on the same comic engine: no money, no colour, and a cast instructed to deliver preposterous lines with flat, over-precise conviction and never signal the joke. The key holds Plan 9 from Outer Space and Ed Wood at this junction, and Cadavra sits between them as the affectionate modern reconstruction rather than the artefact or the biography. What caps it is the objection the previous pass raised against Rubber: Blamire's subject is other films, where McAbee is wholly sincere inside his nonsense. The deadpan itself is an exact match, which is why the tone is a 2 even though the film is a parody.

entries.title: Daisies
entries.what: Věra Chytilová's Czech film: two young women both called Marie decide that since the world has been spoiled they will be spoiled too, and work through a sequence of destructions ending in a wrecked banquet
entries.why: Defensible on construction. Both films are built as a run of set pieces with no narrative obligation between them, both are handmade in a way that keeps showing the seams — Chytilová's tinting, collage and scissored cut-ups against McAbee's painted flats and stage lighting — and both give their protagonists an absurd private rulebook and then simply obey it without comment. Against it: Daisies is riotous, colour-drunk and violent in the cut where the target is still, flat and unhurried, and it is not a musical, which was half the case made for it.

entries.title: The Bed Sitting Room
entries.what: Richard Lester's adaptation of the Spike Milligan and John Antrobus play: survivors of a nuclear war lasting two minutes twenty-eight seconds wander a rubble landscape while some of them mutate into a bed sitting room, a wardrobe and a parrot
entries.why: The closest thing in British cinema to McAbee's method. An impossible premise is stated once, without apology, and then honoured to the letter by actors who behave throughout as though nothing whatever were unusual — a man becoming a chest of drawers is handled as a housing matter. The wasteland is assembled out of genuine junk, false teeth, broken crockery and the dome of St Paul's, exactly the way McAbee builds a solar system out of a barn and some plywood. It belongs with the key's Even Dwarfs Started Small, Greaser's Palace and Putney Swope, and is the better tonal match of the four: dry to the point of melancholy, and funniest when nobody is trying.
